Biden's 81st birthday cake

As of 2025, Biden was the oldest sitting president in U.S. history. His cognitive health was perceived to have declined by Republicans and some media figures,[[680]](#cite_note-701)[[681]](#cite_note-cbsjuly1age-702) and privately by some Democrats. Members of Biden's family and White House staffers insulated Biden from scrutiny of his advanced aging and decline in acuity.[[682]](#cite_note-703)[[683]](#cite_note-wsjagedec-704)[[684]](#cite_note-705)

The media widely covered public concern about Biden's mental acuity after a weak performance in a June 2024 presidential debate,[[681]](#cite_note-cbsjuly1age-702) but gave it limited coverage beforehand, in part due to harsh pushback from White House officials.[[685]](#cite_note-706) Biden initially deemed himself fit to serve two terms as president,[[686]](#cite_note-707) but after the 2024 election said that he may have been too old to serve a second term.[[687]](#cite_note-708)

As part of the [investigation into Biden's handling of classified documents](/wiki/Joe_Biden_classified_documents_incident "Joe Biden classified documents incident"), special counsel [Robert Hur](/wiki/Robert_Hur "Robert Hur") said that Biden did not remember when he was vice president ("if it was 2013—when did I stop being vice president?") or when his son Beau died.[[688]](#cite_note-709) Hur wrote that his memory "appeared to have significant limitations".[[689]](#cite_note-710)

The 1911 statute stated:

> The bear flag is hereby selected and adopted as the state flag of California. ... The said bear flag shall consist of a flag of a length equal to one and one-half the width thereof; the upper five-sixths of the width thereof to be a white field, and the lower sixth of the width thereof to be a red stripe; there shall appear in the white field in the upper left-hand corner a single [red star](/wiki/Red_star "Red star"), and at the bottom of the white field the words '[California Republic](/wiki/California_Republic "California Republic"),' and in the center of the white field a California grizzly bear upon a grass plat, in the position of walking toward the left of the said field; said bear shall be dark brown in color and in length, equal to one-third of the length of said flag.

In 1953, the design and specifications for the state flag were standardized in a bill signed by Governor [Earl Warren](/wiki/Earl_Warren "Earl Warren") and illustrated by Donald Graeme Kelley of Marin County, California.[[5]](#cite_note-5) The Californian state flag is often called the "Bear Flag" and in fact, the present statute adopting the flag, [California Government Code § 420](http://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=420&lawCode=GOV), states: "The Bear Flag is the State Flag of California."

Pursuant to [Section 439 of the California Government Code](http://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=439&lawCode=GOV), the regulations and protocols for the proper display of the flag of California is controlled by the [California Adjutant General](/wiki/California_Adjutant_General "California Adjutant General"):

> The Adjutant General shall, by regulation, prescribe rules regarding the times, places, and the manner in which the State Flag may be displayed. He shall, periodically, compile the laws and regulations regarding the State Flag. Copies of the compilation shall be printed and made available to the public at cost by the Department of General Services.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/GoldenEagleFootLyd4.png/250px-GoldenEagleFootLyd4.png)](/wiki/File:GoldenEagleFootLyd4.png)

The foot and talons of a golden eagle

The golden eagle is a very large raptor, 66 to 102 centimetres (26 to 40 in) in length. Its wings are broad and the wingspan is 1.8 to 2.34 metres (5 ft 11 in to 7 ft 8 in).[[34]](#cite_note-Cornell-34)[[15]](#cite_note-Ferguson-Lees-15)[[35]](#cite_note-35)[[36]](#cite_note-36) The wingspan of golden eagles is the fifth largest among living eagle species.[[15]](#cite_note-Ferguson-Lees-15) [Females are larger than males](/wiki/Sexual_dimorphism "Sexual dimorphism"), with a bigger difference in larger subspecies. Females of the large Himalayan golden eagles are about 37% heavier than males and have nearly 9% longer wings, whereas in the smaller Japanese golden eagles, females are only 26% heavier with around 6% longer wings.[[4]](#cite_note-Watson-4)[[37]](#cite_note-Terres478-37) In the largest subspecies (*A. c. daphanea*), males and females weigh typically 4.05 and 6.35 kg (8.9 and 14.0 lb), respectively. In the smallest subspecies, *A. c. japonica*, males weigh 2.5 kg (5.5 lb) and females 3.25 kg (7.2 lb).[[4]](#cite_note-Watson-4) In the species overall, males average around 3.6 kg (7.9 lb) and females around 5.1 kg (11 lb).[[38]](#cite_note-HBW-38)

The maximum size of golden eagles is debated. Large subspecies are the heaviest representatives of the genus *[Aquila](/wiki/Aquila_(genus) "Aquila (genus)")* and this species is on average the seventh-heaviest living eagle species. The golden eagle is the second heaviest breeding eagle in North America, Europe and Africa and the fourth heaviest in Asia.[[5]](#cite_note-Brown-5)[[15]](#cite_note-Ferguson-Lees-15) For some time, the largest known mass authenticated for a wild female was the specimen from the *A. c. chrysaetos* subspecies which weighed around 6.7 kg (15 lb) and spanned 2.55 m (8 ft 4 in) across the wings.[[22]](#cite_note-Wood-22) American golden eagles are typically somewhat smaller than the large Eurasian species, but a massive female that was banded and relea

A [unicameral parliament](/wiki/Unicameralism "Unicameralism") – known as the **Sabor** – holds [legislative power](/wiki/Legislative_power "Legislative power"). The number of parliament members can vary from 100 to 160. They are elected by popular vote to serve four-year terms. Legislative sessions take place from 15 January to 15 July, and from 15 September to 15 December annually.[[161]](#cite_note-Sabor-about-164) The two largest [political parties in Croatia](/wiki/List_of_political_parties_in_Croatia "List of political parties in Croatia") are the [Croatian Democratic Union](/wiki/Croatian_Democratic_Union "Croatian Democratic Union") (HDZ) and the [Social Democratic Party of Croatia](/wiki/Social_Democratic_Party_of_Croatia "Social Democratic Party of Croatia") (SDP).[[162]](#cite_note-Sabor-MPs-165)

Croatia has a [civil law](/wiki/Civil_law_(legal_system) "Civil law (legal system)") legal system in which law arises primarily from written statutes, with judges serving as implementers and not creators of law. Its development was largely influenced by German and Austrian legal systems. Croatian law is divided into two principal areas—[private](/wiki/Private_law "Private law") and [public law](/wiki/Public_law "Public law"). Before [EU accession negotiations](/wiki/2013_enlargement_of_the_European_Union "2013 enlargement of the European Union") were completed, Croatian legislation had been fully harmonised with the [community acquis](/wiki/Community_acquis "Community acquis").[[163]](#cite_note-DELHRV-overview-166)

In all, 80 nations have [played in at least one World Cup](/wiki/National_team_appearances_in_the_FIFA_World_Cup "National team appearances in the FIFA World Cup").[[n 4]](#cite_note-successor-117) Of these, eight national teams have won the World Cup,[[114]](#cite_note-118) and they have added [stars to their badges](/wiki/Star_(football_badge) "Star (football badge)"), with each star representing a World Cup victory. Uruguay, however, chose to display [four stars on their badge](/wiki/Four_stars_above_Uruguay%27s_football_crest "Four stars above Uruguay's football crest"), representing their two gold medals at the 1924 and 1928 Summer Olympics, which are recognized by FIFA as World Championships, and their two World Cup titles in 1930 and 1950.

With five titles, Brazil are the most successful World Cup team and also the only nation to have [played in every World Cup](/wiki/National_team_appearances_in_the_FIFA_World_Cup#Finals_records_by_team "National team appearances in the FIFA World Cup") (22) to date.[[115]](#cite_note-119) Brazil were also the first team to win the World Cup for the third (1970), fourth (1994) and fifth (2002) time. Italy (1934 and 1938) and Brazil (1958 and 1962) are the only nations to have won consecutive titles. West Germany (1982–1990) and Brazil (1994–2002) are the only nations to appear in three consecutive World Cup finals. Germany has made the most top-four finishes (13), medals (12), as well as the most finals (8).

[George Washington](/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington"), the first president of the United States

As the nation's first president, [George Washington](/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington") established many norms that would come to define the office.[[27]](#cite_note-31)[[28]](#cite_note-32) His decision to retire after two terms helped address fears that the nation would devolve into monarchy and established a precedent that would not be broken until 1940 and would eventually be made permanent by the [Twenty-Second Amendment](/wiki/Twenty-Second_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Twenty-Second Amendment to the United States Constitution"). By the end of his presidency, political parties had developed,[[29]](#cite_note-33) with [John Adams](/wiki/John_Adams "John Adams") defeating [Thomas Jefferson](/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") in 1796, the first truly contested presidential election.[[30]](#cite_note-34) After Jefferson defeated Adams in 1800, he along with [James Madison](/wiki/James_Madison "James Madison") and [James Monroe](/wiki/James_Monroe "James Monroe") would each serve two terms, eventually dominating the nation's politics during the [Era of Good Feelings](/wiki/Era_of_Good_Feelings "Era of Good Feelings") until Adams' son [John Quincy Adams](/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams "John Quincy Adams") won election in 1824 after the [Democratic-Republican Party](/wiki/Democratic-Republican_Party "Democratic-Republican Party") split.

Mike Ross, a university expellee with a [photographic memory](/wiki/Eidetic_memory "Eidetic memory"), makes money by taking the [LSAT](/wiki/Law_School_Admission_Test "Law School Admission Test") and the [bar examination](/wiki/Bar_examination_in_the_United_States "Bar examination in the United States") for others. He does this to pay for his grandmother's living expenses, as she was his primary caregiver after both his parents died in a car accident when he was 11. In the pilot, Mike agrees to deliver a briefcase of [cannabis](/wiki/Cannabis "Cannabis") for his best friend Trevor, a drug dealer, for a large payout. Mike astutely avoids being arrested in a [sting](/wiki/Sting_operation "Sting operation"), only to stumble into a job interview with Harvey Specter, a supremely self-assured [senior partner](/wiki/Partner_(business_rank) "Partner (business rank)") at the prestigious Pearson Hardman, a law firm specializing in [corporate law](/wiki/Corporate_law "Corporate law") and one that only hires [Harvard](/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") graduates. Harvey is impressed by Mike's tenacity and knowledge of the law and hires him as an [associate](/wiki/Associate_attorney "Associate attorney"), despite Mike's not having a license to practice law.[[13]](#cite_note-14) Together they try cases while maintaining Mike's secret from the rest of the firm, though Harvey's insightful [legal secretary](/wiki/Legal_secretary "Legal secretary"), Donna Paulsen, finds out almost immediately. Mike meets Rachel Zane, an ambitious [paralegal](/wiki/Paralegal "Paralegal") he is immediately attracted to, while trying to impress [managing partner](/wiki/Managing_partner "Managing partner") Jessica Pearson and avoid the suspicions of [junior partner](/wiki/Junior_partner "Junior partner") Louis Litt.

[John F. Kennedy](/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy") (1917–1963) and [Nikita Khrushchev](/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev "Nikita Khrushchev") (1894–1971) in [Vienna](/wiki/Vienna "Vienna"), Austria in May 1961

When Kennedy ran for president in 1960, one of his key election issues was an alleged "[missile gap](/wiki/Missile_gap "Missile gap")" with the Soviets. In fact the US at that time was ahead of the Soviets and by an increasingly wide margin. In 1961 the Soviets had four [R-7 Semyorka](/wiki/R-7_Semyorka "R-7 Semyorka") [intercontinental ballistic missiles](/wiki/Intercontinental_ballistic_missile "Intercontinental ballistic missile") (ICBMs); by October 1962, some intelligence estimates indicated a figure of 75.[[35]](#cite_note-afmag-35)

The US had 170 ICBMs and was quickly building more. It also had eight [*George Washington*](/wiki/George_Washington-class_submarine "George Washington-class submarine")- and [*Ethan Allen*-class](/wiki/Ethan_Allen-class_submarine "Ethan Allen-class submarine") [ballistic missile submarines](/wiki/Ballistic_missile_submarine "Ballistic missile submarine"), with the capability to launch 16 [Polaris](/wiki/UGM-27_Polaris "UGM-27 Polaris") missiles, each with a range of 2,500 nautical miles (4,600 km). The Soviet [First Secretary](/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Communist_Party_of_the_Soviet_Union "General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union"), [Nikita Khrushchev](/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev "Nikita Khrushchev"), increased the perception of a 'missile gap' when he boasted to the world that the Soviets were building missiles "like sausages", but Soviet missile numbers and capabilities were nowhere close to his assertions. [Mount Semeru](/wiki/Semeru "Semeru") and [Mount Bromo](/wiki/Mount_Bromo "Mount Bromo") in [East Java](/wiki/East_Java "East Java"). Indonesia's seismic and volcanic activity is among the world's highest.

Indonesia's physical geography is defined by its vast archipelagic extent and varied landscapes. It lies between latitudes [11°S](/wiki/11th_parallel_south "11th parallel south") and [6°N](/wiki/6th_parallel_north "6th parallel north") and longitudes [95°E](/wiki/95th_meridian_east "95th meridian east") and [141°E](/wiki/141st_meridian_east "141st meridian east"),[[87]](#cite_note-Paramita-91) and is the world's largest [archipelagic state](/wiki/Archipelagic_state "Archipelagic state"), stretching 5,120 kilometres (3,181 mi) from east to west and 1,760 kilometres (1,094 mi) from north to south.[[88]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrederickWorden201198-92) This scale makes the surrounding seas central to the country's internal connectivity.[[89]](#cite_note-Oegroseno-93) Several of the archipelago's straits, including [Malacca](/wiki/Malacca_Strait "Malacca Strait"), [Sunda](/wiki/Sunda_Strait "Sunda Strait"), and [Lombok](/wiki/Lombok_Strait "Lombok Strait"), are major maritime chokepoints for regional and global trade, giving Indonesia a strategically important position between the [Indian](/wiki/Indian_Ocean "Indian Ocean") and [Pacific Oceans](/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean").[[89]](#cite_note-Oegroseno-93)[[90]](#cite_note-94)

The six [European Cups](/wiki/UEFA_Champions_League "UEFA Champions League") Liverpool won from 1977 to 2019 on display in the club's museum

In terms of the number of trophies won, Liverpool is regarded as the [most successful club in English football](/wiki/List_of_football_clubs_in_England_by_competitive_honours_won "List of football clubs in England by competitive honours won"). Liverpool's first trophy was the Lancashire League, which it won in the club's first season.[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKelly198815-4) In 1901, the club won its first League title, while the record-equalling twentieth and most recent was in 2025.[[177]](#cite_note-177) Meanwhile, the club's first success in the FA Cup came in 1965. In the 1980s, Liverpool had its most successful decade, when the club won six League titles, two FA Cups, four League Cups, one Football League Super Cup, five [Charity Shields](/wiki/FA_Community_Shield "FA Community Shield") (one shared) and two European Cups. In 2020, Liverpool became the first English club to have won a League title in eight different decades.[[178]](#cite_note-178)

The club has accumulated more [top-flight wins and points](/wiki/Football_records_and_statistics_in_England#Points "Football records and statistics in England") than any other English team.[[179]](#cite_note-179) Liverpool also has the highest average league finishing position (3.3) for the 50-year period from 1965 to 2015,[[180]](#cite_note-180) and second-highest average league finishing position for the period 1900–1999 after [Arsenal](/wiki/Ars

British Shorthair :: Description :: Appearance :: chunk_0005
[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Britskorthaar-64091287828362D7bA.jpg/250px-Britskorthaar-64091287828362D7bA.jpg)](/wiki/File:Britskorthaar-64091287828362D7bA.jpg)

A fully mature male, showing the characteristic heavy jowls, copper-coloured eyes, and unique "crisp" texture of the typical *British Blue* coat.

[![A cat smiling which being scratched behind the ear](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/British_Shorthair_Smiling.jpg/250px-British_Shorthair_Smiling.jpg)](/wiki/File:British_Shorthair_Smiling.jpg)

A British Blue male, showing the classic "[Cheshire Cat](/wiki/Cheshire_Cat "Cheshire Cat") smile" for which the breed is renowned.

The British Shorthair is a large, powerful-looking cat with a broad chest, sturdy, thick-set legs, and rounded paws. The body is muscular and well boned, supported by medium to short legs and finished with round, medium-to-large feet. The tail is medium in length, thick at the base and tapering to a rounded tip, measuring roughly two-thirds of the body length.[[15]](#cite_note-CFAstandard-15)[[16]](#cite_note-TICAstd-16)

The head is large and distinctly rounded, with a short muzzle, full cheeks—especially pronounced in mature males—and a short nose with a gentle profile. The chin and muzzle complement the circular head shape, while the neck blends into the cheeks, creating the impression of little or no visible neck. The ears are small to medium in size, broad at the base and set widely apart. The eyes are large, round, and level-set; eye shape is considered more important than colour. In the British Blue they are typically deep copper-orange, while other coat varieties may show different eye colours.[[15]](#cite_note-CFAstandard-15)[[16]](#cite_note-TICAstd-16)

British Shorthairs mature relatively slowly, reaching full physical development at around three years of age. Unusually among domestic cats, they are a noticeably sexually dimorphic breed, with males averaging 4–8 kg (9–17 lb) and females 3–5 kg (7–12 lb).[[17]](#cite_note-CFAintro-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18)

Emmanuelle Charpentier :: Early life and education :: chunk_0001
Charpentier's paternal grandfather, surnamed Sinanian, was an [Armenian](/wiki/Armenians "Armenians") who escaped to France during the [Armenian Genocide](/wiki/Armenian_Genocide "Armenian Genocide") and met his wife in [Marseille](/wiki/Marseille "Marseille").[[7]](#cite_note-Public_Radio_of_Armenia-7) Charpentier was born in 1968 in [Juvisy-sur-Orge](/wiki/Juvisy-sur-Orge "Juvisy-sur-Orge") in France and studied biochemistry, microbiology, and genetics at the [Pierre and Marie Curie University](/wiki/Pierre_and_Marie_Curie_University "Pierre and Marie Curie University") (which became the Faculty of Science of [Sorbonne University](/wiki/Sorbonne_University "Sorbonne University")) in Paris.[[8]](#cite_note-mpg-vita-8) She was a graduate student at the [Institut Pasteur](/wiki/Institut_Pasteur "Institut Pasteur") from 1992 to 1995 and was awarded a research doctorate. Charpentier's PhD work investigated molecular mechanisms involved in [antibiotic resistance](/wiki/Antimicrobial_resistance "Antimicrobial resistance").[[9]](#cite_note-9)
